Title: The Song of the Cell: An Exploration of Medicine and the New Human
Author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
My Review:
_The Song of the Cell_

Another dive into the discoveries of and in cell biology by Siddhartha Mukherjee. Perhaps a gentler read than his introduction to cancer biology.

Just as atoms are the basic units of matter, the cell is the unit of all living things. Every process of life, normal and malignant, can be understood through the behaviour of cells. We have encountered this idea in school, but rarely did we pause to appreciate the enigma of it. How a cell forms tissue, tissue forms organs, and organs form a system so precise in its roles, rules, and responses that every act of being alive is, on reflection, nothing short of wonder.

Mukherjee begins with Leeuwenhoek’s first observation of cells, then moves through the competing theories of how cells were thought to function, grounding each leap in the experimental evidence and the details of the setups that made the next understanding possible.

From there, the book traces cell modification and gene therapy all the way to IVF, the birth of the first test-tube baby, the decades of research behind it, and the scientific, political, and religious undercurrents that surrounded the invention. Then further still, to gene-editing technologies and He Jiankui, the Chinese researcher who in 2018 announced the birth of the first gene-edited babies. I remember reading about his subsequent arrest in the papers. That episode illuminated just how much ethical, moral, and scientific transparency matters and how its absence made the development of global protocols not just necessary, but urgent.

We also learn about the discovery of insulin, a Nobel-winning breakthrough, awarded to Frederick Banting and John Macleod in 1923. Banting, feeling his research assistant Charles Best deserved equal credit, shared his prize money with him.
Moving to Shinya Yamanaka’s landmark discovery, that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2012. The reversal of any cell back to its stem cell state, a kind of biological time warp. A divided, specialised cell walked backwards, reprogrammed into virtually any cell of choice. It is a finding that upended one of transplantation’s oldest and most brutal problems: histoincompatibility. The immune system is exquisitely tuned to recognise self from non-self, and for decades that precision worked against us donor organs attacked and destroyed by the very body they were meant to save. The ability to reprogramme a patient’s own cells sidesteps that rejection entirely, and remains quietly extraordinary.

The book closes on cancer, and on why it is no longer enough to study cells in isolation. Context matters: what surrounds a cell, what signals it receives, what position it holds. It raises questions like why, despite the liver and spleen sitting in close proximity, cancer metastasis appears in the liver but almost never in the spleen.

So much remains to be understood. What we do know has come from decades of disciplined, painstaking work by researchers, doctors, nurses, and patients each contributing to a collective effort to understand something as fundamental as ourselves. Without that drive to study the basic unit of life, there would be no treatments, no vaccines, nothing.

PS: If The Emperor of All Maladies is where you want to arrive, this book offers the better starting point. Cells first.

“If you were to build the world again, to create males and females again, do not be like an inexperienced potter. Come to earth as a woman, Prabhu!
Be a woman once, oh Lord!” #banumushtaq

Banu Mushtaq’s #heartlamp won the 2025 booker prize. Her 12 stories are not of empowered women but of the quiet strength of women. The kind of strength not demanding to be witnessed or felt. Mushtaq’s women linger, refusing closure, leaving behind the weight of unresolved justice.

Even though the stories are grounded in a specific religion and community, the theme is universal. Violence, silence, survival and grief are after all universal. Translated by #deepabhasti, the discomfort is not smoothed over, rather the tension is felt by the reader.

Title: The Lowland
Author: Jhumpa Lahiri
My Review:
_The Lowland_

Set against the backdrop of the 1960s Naxalite movement in Calcutta, The Lowland traces the lives of two brothers whose childhood closeness slowly gives way to distance shaped by choice, conviction, and circumstance.

Once inseparable, their paths diverge sharply in early adulthood. Yet the quiet gravity of family has its own pull, drawing their lives back into one another in ways that are complicated, fragile, and enduring. Each must live with the weight of what was chosen and what was left behind.

Lahiri writes about life not as tragedy, but as it unfolds: restrained, intimate, and deeply human. Her prose moves with a quiet poetry tinged with a gentle melancholy.

Title: Old God's Time
Author: Sebastian Barry
My Review:
“Not just as a point of official principle, but as a secret, private principle that all children must be guarded. They must have safety and if they could also have love, so much the better. To threaten a child, to bring hurt to a child, was the chief crime before God and man. It must never go un-punished. A child was a small matter by definition. Who will speak for the child? Who will act for him or her?”#sebastianbarry

Old God’s Time by Sebastian Barry (2023) is set against the backdrop of Irish Catholic institutional abuse. We meet Tom Kettle, a retired detective and survivor of childhood abuse. We live through the lifelong trauma of his experience and its generational effects. Tom’s and his wife’s trauma does not simply vanish, despite their best efforts. It percolates, seeps into everyday life, and spills into the lives of their children.

It’s a classic example of an unreliable narrator—the story unfolds entirely within the narrator’s mind, through his thoughts and perceptions. That is all we are given at first. Gradually, through his rambling reflections, we begin to realize that not everything presented to us is true. Some parts reflect what he wishes were true, some verge on hallucination, and others seem to gloss over the harsher realities of his life.

In this subtle and compelling way, we come to understand the protagonist’s life—his family, his childhood, and his youth.

He is ultimately forced to confront and accept the harsh life he was dealt, despite his persistent attempts to suppress and erase those painful memories.

It’s a slow read and may not be everyone’s taste. But if you enjoy living inside and slowly detangling through another person’s mind, then this is for you.

Title: Wolf Hall (Thomas Cromwell, #1)
Author: Hilary Mantel
My Review:
« Why are we so attached to the severities of the past? Why are we so proud of having endured our fathers and our mothers, the fireless days and the meatless days, the cold winters and the sharp tongues? It's not as if we had a choice. » #hilarymantel

A masterpiece by Hilary Mantel and winner of the Booker Prize, Wolf Hall is the first part of a trilogy narrating the rise of Thomas Cromwell from a humble blacksmith’s son to Prime Minister to Henry VIII.

This part follows the political and religious manoeuvres used to legitimise Henry’s marriage to Anne Boleyn, from pressuring the Church and bending the law to slowly dismantling the authority of Rome itself in order to nullify his decades-long marriage to Catherine of Aragon.

It’s historical fiction that reads like a slow political thriller. Rich in detail and a taxing read, but I enjoyed it thoroughly. I love well-researched, immersive historical fiction, and mix politics into it and it’s sold for me. Mantel brings remarkable depth to the character of Cromwell, who otherwise survives in history mostly through the records of Henry VIII.

If you enjoy power, politics, and drama moving like a game of chess, then this is for you.

Here’s a quick context to Henry VIII’s court.

P.S. Henry breaks from Rome to marry Anne Boleyn, with Anne herself playing a part in the scheming and isolation of Catherine of Aragon. But the same ruthless court politics that crown her eventually lead to her execution on Henry’s orders.

Title: The Emperor of All Maladies: A Biography of Cancer
Author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
My Review:
Death in old age is inevitable, but death before old age is not.”
— Richard Doll, quoted in The Emperor of All Maladies

A Pulitzer Prize winning novel by Sidharth Mukherjee, the book is a biography of cancer. Mukherjee, a cancer physician and researcher, traces cancer from Imhotep’s admission of helplessness to the molecular age’s understanding the function and structure of cancer cells. While occasionally meandering, it is an essential reading for patients, physicians, and anyone who has ever sat in a waiting room trying to find the right words.


Cancer cells are not alien, they arise from within, carrying our own DNA, running our own growth machinery, only without the brakes. This likeness is why cancer is so hard to treat. Every drug that kills a cancer cell risks killing a normal one. The therapeutic window is narrow because the biological distance between us and our tumours is small.

The striking insight by Mukherjee was reframing the whole ambition of oncology: not cure, but the right to reach old age. A cancer rendered chronic may be the most honest definition of winning, that medicine can currently offer.

“Indeed, as the fraction of those affected by cancer creeps inexorably in some nations from one in four to one in three to one in two, cancer will, indeed, be the new normal. The question then will not be if we will encounter this immortal illness in our lives, but when.”

Title: The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida
Author: Shehan Karunatilaka
My Review:
_The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida_

“Even on the sad days, when you have to process young children or those leaving lovers behind, you come to realise that every death is significant, even when every life appears not to be”
Shehan Karunatilaka, The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida


It is 1990, Colombo, Sri Lanka. Maali Almeida is dead and he has seven moons or 7 nights to find out the why’s, who’s and how’s about his death.

In his life, he was a professional war photographer, specifically Sri lankan civil war. During his lifetime, Maali was not particularly concerned with the ethics or morality either in professional or personal life. He worked for anyone who interested him, his main objective being to gather intelligence photographs which he believed would help in ending the war and toppling down the government.

The writing style reminds me a little of Salman Rushdie with heavy magical realism interspersed with political satire and historical context. Narrated in second person style, #shehankarunatilaka takes us through the darkest periods of Srilankan history.

The author boldly writes about the various warring factions within Sri Lanka and the international armies and intelligence agencies who enter with the promise of aid but contribute as much to the existing civil unrest.

The narrative does fall a little slow and repetitive at times, but not enough to stop reading. It is immersive, compelling and a powerful story. Worthy of the 2022 international booker prize.

Title: Creation Lake
Author: Rachel Kushner
My Review:
_Creation Lake_

#creationlake by #rachelkushner is shortlisted for the booker prize 2024. The book is from the perspective of a secret agent ‘Sadie Smith’ sent by private anonymous agents to investigate a commune in rural French, led by a strange man Bruno Lacombe, who communicates only via email.
Bruno is obsessed with the Neanderthal way of life and strongly believes that homosapien’s modern life resulted in the mess we are in. He advocates for a return to ancient life. Her agents want her to dig out some dirt on the commune to incarcerate them, subsequently provoke them to incite violence and sometimes more.

Although designed as a spy thriller, it is anything but a fast paced thriller. We are introduced to Sadie smith and how Bruno Lacombe’s ideas, sometimes even ridiculous ones seem to influence her. And in this process, we are allowed a glimpse to the true nature of Sadie Smith. The novel is interspersed with the retrospections of her past assignments and Bruno Lacombe’s emails. Complexity of Sadie’s character is a highlight in the book and so is the philosophical discussion via Bruno’s emails about why Homo sapiens emerged dominant.

The book is mix of spy life and philosophy. Sadie is sarcastic, clever and humorous while Bruno presents a touch of intellectual stimulation. It’s the discussion itself and the character arc of Sadie that forms the crux of the book.

I enjoyed it but I thought the ending fell a little flat.

Title: The Memory Police
Author: Yōko Ogawa
My Review:
_The Memory Police_

The memory police is a compelling book published 25 years ago in Japan and recently translated to English in 2019. The book was shortlisted for international booker prize in 2020.

There is a writer in an unnamed island that none are able to depart. Things disappear in the island routinely. Birds, calendar, flowers, books etc, and when they disappear, any memory associated with that object also disappears from the inhabitant’s life. Soon they can no longer remember the object, any memory of it or any sense of what it might have been at all.

There are people in the island, who can remember. They are rounded up by the memory police and taken away.

The book is very subtle, the premise although sounds structured, soon becomes a vague exploration of what it means to not have memories. How it may shape our sense of self. There is no discussion of why, how or when the disappearing happens. Ogawa’s words are calm and flat while they detail unnerving events.

The protagonist’s boss who can still remember, reassures that disappearance doesn’t necessarily mean it stops existing. There is a quite tension between the need to remember and the opportunity to not remember. Thus those who forget don’t have a sense of loss. Because it ceases to exist for them. We are left to wonder if it’s really so bad to not have memories.

Ogawa offers no answers just a lot of questions in your head. Do memories shape communities, our sense of self? If we could collectively forget, what does it mean for us as a community. Is life easier ? The work can be experienced as fable or allegory, warning and illumination. A rare piece of writing.

Title: The Three-Body Problem (Remembrance of Earth’s Past, #1)
Author: Liu Cixin
My Review:
_The Three Body Problem_

The trilogy is a translated Chinese fiction consisting of *The Three-Body Problem*, *The Dark Forest*, and *Death’s End*.

The “three-body problem” is an actual physics issue that deals with the chaotic and unpredictable movements of three celestial bodies in space. In the book, the Trisolarans come from a civilization in a three-star system, which creates an extremely unstable environment for them. To survive, they must find another habitable planet.

When Earth's location is broadcast, the Trisolarans begin their journey toward us, but they are still 450 years away. The book deeply explores how human society might react to the knowledge of an impending doomsday centuries away, examining social, technological, and scientific implications.

The philosophical questions raised in *The Three-Body Problem* are especially thought-provoking. How would contact with an alien civilization change humanity? Is coexistence possible? Would the awareness of such a future increase the divide or form a catalyst for a newer just society? And who bears the burden of this new reality—us, or the future generations?

In the second book, the “dark forest theory” is introduced, highlighting the dangers of a civilization broadcasting its location. It is one of many possible explanations of the Fermi paradox. The paradox states that If we assume that the solar system is typical of the billions and billions of similar systems, then where is everyone?

Cixin Liu presents a grim view of life in the universe: with so many planets, life likely exists beyond Earth, but the galaxy is eerily silent. He compares it to a dark forest, where civilizations hide to avoid detection. Revealing your location could invite immediate threats from more advanced civilizations. The Trisolarans are one such threat, but there are likely others.

The final book raises a profound question: are the physical laws of the universe we study are natural, or are they shaped by civilizations?

The trilogy spans centuries, beginning with humanity's awareness of the Trisolarans’ approach, through a truce between the two species, and beyond. It’s rich with scientific detail, which might be daunting for some readers, but as a science enthusiast, I found it incredibly rewarding. While the character development is lacking—possibly due to translation—the depth and detail more than make up for it.

Overall, it’s one of the finest works of science fiction I’ve read.

Title: In Ascension
Author: Martin MacInnes
My Review:
_In Ascension_

“In order to create itself, life already has to exist. The end instigates a beginning. Cells produce the conditions essential for their own creation. Life is circular, atemporal. Every cell an instance of time travel. “

Long listed for the 2023 Booker Prize, #inascension is Martin Macinnes ambitious work exploring a human life. From the deep vents discovered in ocean to the farthest reaches of Solar System, the book is a journey of a Life specifically of Dr Leigh Hasenboch, who trained as a marine microbiologist.

A compassionate, inquisitive epic, it’s a unique blend of exploring the big questions set in the background of innate human fragility.

I love books that expound science, and this one did it while being a mixed genre. It was intellectually interesting and stimulating. This book may not be for everyone. There are pages and pages of subtle layering which you may not like if you are into fast paced sci-fiction novellas. This is a soft science-fiction (a very very near future), not dystopian, amply interspersed with psychology and philosophy (If you liked Arrival or Interstellar or Space Odyssey, then you may like this).

The mystery is not solved, rather its existence is revealed. It gives something that you carry with you long after you finish the book.

“Everyone should be acknowledged. Everyone should be missed when they are not right there with you because of what they carry, this very distinct way they have of bearing themselves that is like no one else and that is built by everything they have done and everything they have seen.”

Title: Time Shelter
Author: Georgi Gospodinov
My Review:
_Time Shelter_

"It's simple. When you have no future, you vote for the past."

Bulgarian author Georgi Gospodinov's "Time Shelter," translated to English by Angela Rodel, portrays a geriatric psychiatrist named Gaustine who treats dementia patients using ‘clinics of the past’ recreating detailed historical settings. This concept soon expands to influence European politics. Europe decides to go back to a past where they believe they had the best times.

The novel develops this into a Brexit model where each country decides to which decade from the 20th century they would like to return. This is the best part in the book, as the narrator walks through the choices in each country.

It’s a clever and powerful reflection of our political present, particularly how nostalgia is wielded to push specific agendas.

"The aging chose the years of their youth, yet the young, who were not even born then, would have to live in those years. There was a certain injustice in that - choosing the time the next generation would live in. As happens in all elections, actually."

The novel prioritizes ideas over characters, plot, or setting, occasionally meandering chaotically. Despite this, I found it enjoyable. What's noteworthy is its non-hypothetical nature; we've all heard political calls to return to a glorified past we didn't experience firsthand.

Title: Small Great Things
Author: Jodi Picoult
My Review:
_Small Great Things_

“Equality is treating everyone the same. But equity is taking differences into account, so everyone has a chance to succeed.” #jodipicolt

This work by Jodi Picolt is about an African American labor and delivery Nurse with over 20 years experience being accused of the murder of a baby by its white supremacist father.

The book is a layered and empathetic exploration of race in the contemporary world. It poses a particular position that the protagonist Ruth finds herself in. And in exploring this unique situation, Jodi Picolt addresses equality and equity and the subtle ways passive racism moves among us. Jodi takes a step further and provides a background for the white suprimacist father, portraying his journey to his ideals. Picolt’s work doesn’t preach, instead it simply pulls up a mirror and forces you to acknowledge the many many privileges that we take for granted.

The ending was perhaps idyllic, but over all, the book was a good exposition of race in the modern world and gives the reader a lot to reflect upon.

“You say you don’t see color…but that’s all you see. You’re so hyperaware of it, and of trying to look like you aren’t prejudiced, you can’t even understand that when you say race doesn’t matter all I hear is you dismissing what I’ve felt, what I’ve lived, what it’s like to be put down because of the color of my skin.”

Title: Nine Lives: In Search of the Sacred in Modern India
Author: William Dalrymple
My Review:
_Nine Lives: In Search of the Sacred in Modern India_

“There is no fire in hell,” he reported. “Everyone who goes there brings their own fire, and their own pain, from this world.” #williamdalrympal

William Dalrymple's 'Nine Lives' begins by introducing a nomadic Jain Nun in Sravanabelagola who had to watch her friend ritually starve herself to death, then it traverses through the Theyyam dancers of Kerala, Sufism in Sindh, a Tibetian monk who had to take up arms, the bronze idol makers of Swamimalai, Devadasis in Saundatti, Karnataka and Tantrists in Bengal. Nine magically crafted live stories is told by Dalrympal as an observer who lets the characters tell their spellbinding stories. Each of these people are intensely invested in their faiths.

Rituals and traditions run deep in India and it is an illustration of how much modernisation and the sacred co exist in this complex nation. What is God in their eyes is beautiful, generous and kind. In these lives religion becomes a simple faith and not an institution and that makes all the difference.

Title: The Reader
Author: Bernhard Schlink
My Review:
_The Reader_

#thereader is an emotionally intelligent novel on the connection between morality, responsibility and the degrees to which we think are responsible for the world.

Originally written in German, it is translated to English by #carolbrownjaneway, it is simultaneously powerful and philosophical and yet not unrealistic or uncommon.

It tackles many aspects, one of which is Holocaust weighing in on a post-war generation of Germany. It is also about illiteracy and its weight on a person, about how far can a person go to protect their ego, about the affair between the young protagonist and an older woman and it’s effect on the protagonist’s life. It is about blind obedience and the sort of helpless it generates. It’s a juxtaposition of many aspects.

The writing questions the mankind: what is to be done with the knowledge of the horrors of Holocaust. Do we feel guilt, or shame, or sadness. What do we do with it ? Could any person be considered guilty if they knew about the camps but did nothing ? These questions, like the question to the judge ("... so what would you have done?"), lingers and floats in mid-air.

The character of Hanna Schmidt is quite remarkable and engrossing. The book, its musings and Hanna Schmidt stay with you, perhaps forever only as questions without any answers.

“I wanted to pose myself both tasks - understanding and condemnation. But it was impossible to do both” #bernhardschlink

Title: To Kill a Mockingbird
Author: Harper Lee
My Review:
_To Kill a Mocking Bird_

“ There are just some kind of men who - who're so busy worrying about the next world they've never learned to live in this one, and you can look down the street and see the results.” #harperlee

#tokillamockingbird is a 6 year old child’s perspective of her father’s stand against racial injustice during the 1930’s Deep South of USA.

Here is a fine novel filled with beautiful details and clearly layered characters. The wise yet weary Atticus Finch, Scout and Jem's widowed father, is a noble, warm man who frequently displays a wealth of compassion and empathy which he lovingly imparts to his two children.

Every line in the book is filled with a deep sense of life, warmth and raw humour. The children’s exploration of the society’s irrationality and attitudes to race and gender pricks your conscience.

A must, to meet Atticus Finch once in your life.

Title: What Is Life? with Mind and Matter and Autobiographical Sketches
Author: Erwin Schrödinger
My Review:
_What is Life_

Dive into the essence of life with Erwin Schrödinger's 1944 non-fiction gem, "What is Life." Stemming from Schrödinger's captivating lectures at Trinity College in 1943, the book transcends the conventional divide between biology and the physical sciences.

Schrodinger, with this book, discussing his brilliant intuitions and observations, partly inspired the men and women 10 years later to uncover the double helix structure and form of the DNA.

Schrödinger addressed what puzzled many students — why biology was treated as a subject completely separate from physics and chemistry: On one side were living organisms like animals, plants and cells, while on the other were the realms of atoms, molecules, electricity, and magnetism.

He put a physicist’s question to biology. If entropy is (according to the second law of thermodynamics) things falling apart, the natural disintegration of order into disorder, why don’t genes decay? Why are they instead passed intact from generation to generation? Schrödinger posits that life can resist entropy because of metabolism i.e. life’s ability to draw upon organic compounds which serve them as foodstuffs to maintain order.

In the second half of the book, Schrodinger, observes Life through the prism of metaphysics contemplating consciousness, mind, matter, and the frontiers of scientific understanding.

A riveting conclusion to the literary journey of 2023.

#erwinschrodinger #whatislife #nonfiction #science

Title: The Promise
Author: Damon Galgut
My Review:
_The Promise_

“Apartheid has fallen, see, we die right next to each other now, in intimate proximity. It's just the living part we still have to work out.” #damungalgut

Winner of the 2021 booker prize, ‘The Promise’ by Damon Galgut charts the slow decline of a white South African family comprising of Ma, Pa and their three children (Anton, Astrid, Amor).

The title refers to the promise made by Manie (Pa) to his dying wife Rachel (Ma), overheard by their youngest daughter Amor, that their black family maid Salome should inherit the tiny house in their farm which she currently occupies.

However, at Ma’s funeral, upon reminded of the promise, he refuses having made any, and the promise is skipped over.

The book spans over 4 decades, with each of the 4 chapter looking at the death of one of the family member and the political and personal changes that the decade has brought. At each funeral, the subject of the promise is brought up by Amor and passed off, refused or remains without any action by the characters.

The book is wonderfully written with a omniscient third person narration, with the perspectives shifting fluidly between the thoughts of characters, sometimes random objects. The narration is fast and each funeral brings a heaviness that is in stark contrast to the fluid narration.

The black characters remain obscure in the book, their thoughts, history and life quite missing in the narration. And this is deliberate, a subtle way of showing their invisibility to the white gaze. It has a dark humour under a melancholy undertone that slowly weighs you down.

Perhaps not a Christmassy book in the usual sense, but still one of hope and redemption.

PS: “No love left, only kindness”

Title: The Heart of a Dog
Author: Mikhail Bulgakov
My Review:
“Nobody should be whipped. Remember that, once and for all. Neither man nor animal can be influenced by anything but suggestion” #mikhailbulgakov

‘The heart of a dog/ A dog’s heart’ is a satire on 1920’s Russian society and the their idea of a Soviet man.

A street dog ‘Sharik’ is picked up by a medical professor and is changed into a man after a blotched transplant operation.
The professor represents everything the Russian revolutionary regime wishes to eradicate and Sharik the ‘new man’ is the example of everything that ruins Russia according to Bulgakov. Sharik’s integration into soviet society is written as a clever comment on Russian revolution, the class discrepancies and the rise of the proletariat.

Bulgakovs short book makes for a rewarding read. The manuscript of the book was confiscated shortly after it was written and not published until 40 years after.

PS: “One can find time for everything if one is never in a hurry”

Title: Permanent Record
Author: Edward Snowden
My Review:
_Permanent Record_

“Technology doesn’t have a Hippocratic oath. So many decisions that have been made by technologists in academia, industry, the military, and government since at least the Industrial Revolution have been made on the basis of “can we,” not “should we.” And the intention driving a technology’s invention rarely, if ever, limits its application and use…” #edwardsnowden

In 2013, 29 year old Edward Snowden released documents revealing America’s highly secret and unprecedented system of mass surveillance. He disclosed numerous surveillance programs developed and used in collaboration with the ‘Five Eyes’ Intelligence alliance i.e an alliance comprising of Canada, Australia, New Zealand, UK and USA and also shared among other European countries.

His actions led to the debate of ‘individual privacy’ and national security. Subsequently a couple of reforms including data encryption standards for file transfers and newer data protection policies were developed.

Snowden’s autobiography is a quick and engaging read explaining the moments that led to his decision to disclose. It’s written in simple prose with technical content explained lucidly with analogies for lay person to comprehend.

Read it if you are interested in conversations on digital privacy.


PS: “Ultimately, saying that you don’t care about privacy because you have nothing to hide is no different from saying you don’t care about freedom of speech because you have nothing to say…”

Title: Fatherland
Author: Robert   Harris
My Review:
_Fatherland_

An alternate history 1992 novel by #robertharris, Fatherland talks about a setting where Nazis won the World War II. Nazi Germany has taken over most of Europe and is locked in a Cold War with US. The author has done good research and characters are drawn from the original high ranking Nazis and projected into this alternate history. The city of Berlin in this book is the Berlin that Albert Speer, a German architect and close ally of Hitler, planned to build.

Peripherally it begins as a procedural detective story but soon takes up the bigger political cover up of what exactly happened to the Europe’s Jews (There are whispers and speculations but they are pushed aside as American propaganda)

It is a good read and a fairly good representation of what might Germany look like in this Alternate history and how the whole of Europe would be as a result and of-course Germany’s relationship with US.

While the protagonist and his love interest lack lustre as characters and show no depth, it is the entire setting that kept me engaged. Despite the interesting premise, the writing is sometimes boring. I suppose the book’s achievement lies in its presentation of this alternate history more than being a thriller.

Title: The House in the Cerulean Sea (Cerulean Chronicles, #1)
Author: T.J. Klune
My Review:
_The House in the Cerulean Sea_

#thehouseintheceruleansea is a simple story about acceptance and inclusivity. It has mutant children isolated from society and cared for by special homes.

The protagonist Linus Baker is an employee at DICOMY (Dept in charge for magical youth) whose job involves inspecting how the special homes are run. He is assigned with a task to visit a top secret location housed by 6 supposedly dangerous children and inspect its running.

It is a simple feel-good ‘read by the beach on a sunny day’ type of light fantasy book. The writing was fluid and uncomplicated with some very memorable characters. I loved the child ‘Chauncey’ who dreams of becoming a bellhop.

I felt the book could be more layered and the characters explored more. At the moment, it feels too simple, predictable and unoriginal (it’s very much like X-men) but nevertheless well written. The author has chosen to limit the discussion to the overarching theme of prejudice and people in power abusing their role in protecting the marginalised. The characters could be flushed out in more detail and used to drive the plot line. It felt like all the characters had a great introduction but fell short of a middle and and end, leaving you with a missing feeling.

TJ Klune has a writing style with an essence of Douglas Adams and Terry Pratchett. The book is recommended for cozy feel good weekend vibes.

Title: Victory City
Author: Salman Rushdie
My Review:
_Victory City_

“History is the consequence not only of people’s actions, but also of their forgetfulness” #salmanrushdie

In #victorycity Rushdie returns to magical realism, myth, and India’s ancient stories. Typical of his style, his extensive research on historical facts are liberally spiked with magic to create his masterpiece. But unlike his previous works, #victorycity is easy to read, moving linearly and focussing on one character arc.

Victory city (based on the medieval Indian Kingdom of Vijayanagara, which rose and fell from 1336–1565), is styled as an abridged translation of an epic narrated by the fictional character of Pampa Kampana who is given the gift of creating an empire with seeds and whisperings. The story chronicles the rise and fall of the ‘victory city’ (translation of the word Vijayanagara), forever oscillating between better and worse. It’s not difficult to see that it’s an allegory for present-day India narrated by a resilient female demigod.

The book touches a lot of themes from religious intolerance, weaponisation of religion in politics, pluralism and gender inequality.
Rushdie impresses upon readers the power of imaginative storytelling and iterates that what remains at the end is words. Rushdie elevates those who wield the power of words to a god like importance. It is their liberal words alone that stands as a witness to all that existed before our time. What is true, what is fiction, what is important and what is not, is given to us to sift through.

“Words are the only victors,” reads its last line.

Title: Anxious People
Author: Fredrik Backman
My Review:
_Anxious People_

“They say that a person’s personality is the sum of their experiences. But that isn’t true, at least not entirely, because if our past was all that defined us, we’d never be able to put up with ourselves. We need to be allowed to convince ourselves that we’re more than the mistakes we made yesterday. That we are all of our next choices, too, all of our tomorrows.” #fredrikbackman

Backman writes on being human, on how stupid, quirky and sentimental we all are. And his writings combine these elements, that both makes you laugh and feel belonged. I have always enjoyed reading books that introduce complex humanness through whimsical or humorous writing style and I liked this one just as much as #amancalledove.

Very simply the book is about a bank robbery gone wrong and an accidental hostage situation involving a very reluctant and confused robber and a bunch of people who are ‘the worst hostages ever’.

It can be a little wordy which may not be to everyone’s taste, but I find whimsically written long texts pretty amusing.

“You need psychology if you think you're a dolphin. You need psychiatry if you've killed all the dolphins” #fredrikbackman

Title: The White Castle
Author: Orhan Pamuk
My Review:
_The White Castle_

Translated from the Turkish by Victoria Holbrook, the book is Orhan Pamuk’s exploration on identity. Set in the 17th century, two men find themselves sharing facial similarity. A young Italian explorer is taken as slave by a Turkish court scholar who looks like his double.

They begin by exchanging ideas on science, medicine and astronomy. But as years progress their identities blur, each taking on aspects of the other’s persona.
Orhan Pamuk writes a short treatise where he asks, given knowledge about each others intricate details in life, can you exchange your life with another ?

There are events described like that of the onset of Plague and how the two scholars deal with it and the subtle fears of a man who worries if he is losing his identity, that are remarkable to read. But on the whole, it reads more like a monotonic memoir of the protagonist. It raises interesting questions which if you think too much is bound to give you a head ache and precisely for that reason, it was an illuminating read albeit a little dry writing.

Title: Airframe
Author: Michael Crichton
My Review:
_Airframe_

Airframe details an investigation by an aircraft manufacturing industry Norton, after a mid-air plane disaster that killed three passengers and injured 56 others.

It was weak as a thriller, but as an aviation investigation with deep scientific and technical introduction to aircraft manufacturing and maintenance the book is wonderful. It is a typical Crichton book involving a surprisingly complex subject and detailing it in an engaging way for readers. Additionally, he also explores media exploitations and their way of going for ‘sensational’ news rather than true details. The book has a good reflection of media landscape illustrating TV anchors quoting out of context and presenting only half the information leading to a seriously biased view of any incident. It is a good example of how difficult it can be to explain complex technical works while the media meticulously refuses to engage in understanding with their interest solely focused on driving the interviewee to an already established ‘sensational’ news angle.

If you are into learning about aviation industry, then this book is for you. If you are looking for action packed thriller, then this is definitely not that despite the misleading synopsis which is simply tip of the iceberg.

Michael Crichton has never disappointed me. Once again I enjoyed the scientific rigour and the many questions he raises.

Title: The Satanic Verses
Author: Salman Rushdie
My Review:
_The Satanic Verses_

“The fact of being alive compensated for what life did to one” #salmanrushdie

Rushdie once again weaves magic with his words. The book is highly imaginative multi-layered tale seeped in magical realism which is typical of Rushdie’s style.

Particularly in this book, the exposition of various ideas is much like rolling a dice. There is nationalism, immigrant identity, ideas of good and evil, perspectives on blind faith and so much more.

Rushdie paints a unique portrait where perhaps world view and social constructs are as much a part of our individual identity. Sometimes some elements are part of our identity simply because we aim to resist it and the resistance becomes our sense of self. If we were not resisting ideas which we believe need a reform, what sort of idea would we be ?

The story follows an Indian actor Gibreel and a London based voice-over artist Chamcha. The story begins when the protagonists find themselves transformed to the images of an Angel and a Satan respectively. Their metamorphosis reflects their inner struggles. Chamcha has always struggled to integrate as an immigrant in London where they refuse to accept him despite him vehemently shedding his Indianness. While Gibreel, basked in his glory as an actor does not comprehend his deteriorating mental health stemming from his narcissistic tendencies.

Through their transformations and subsequent narratives modelled in the form of dream sequences and real-time incidents, Rushdie writes magic.

Title: The Lion and the Puppy: And Other Stories for Children
Author: Leo Tolstoy
My Review:
_The Lion and the Puppy_

Little known stories written by Leo Tolstoy for the children in Tolstoy's school in the village.

They are very interesting in that it stands in contrast to the typical children’s books you come across. These are not simple moral stories with happy endings. In fact there were very few with what you might call as happy endings and ideal closures.
The stories reflect a sense of melancholy expounding that sometimes inexplicably sad things may happen in life but sort of also elegantly paints that life may be bigger than all of them and still worth moving ahead.

While it may be difficult to expound the stories to children, I feel it opens up excellent discussions and questions rather than the typical spoon feeding of black and white morals.

Title: Alias Grace
Author: Margaret Atwood
My Review:
_Alias Grace_

“If we were all on trial for our thoughts, we would all be hanged.” #margaretatwood

In 1843, 16 year old Grace Marks with fellow servant James McDermott was convicted for her involvement in the murders of her employer Thomas Kinnear and housekeeper Nancy.

Grace was sentenced to life imprisonment and McDermott was hanged. The plot is based on a real Canadian murder case.

This is all the facts we have and the rest of the book is a question of Grace’s guilt or innocence. The plot is permeated by the class distinctions and immigrant migration of 19th century. Atwood writes devastating accounts of poverty, starvation and the powerlessness of being a woman on top of that.

It’s not a conventional true crime thriller. It’s more than that. Alias Grace is less about finding the truth about the murders and more about unlayering the mild mannered Grace and her life told by numerous voices including her own, Dr Jordan, news paper cuttings, other letters and articles of the time. The result is a stunning portrait of Grace Marks marked by her life as a poor Irish immigrant in the 19 century.

Contrary to a fast paced murder mystery, the book is slower and colder and was a more satisfactory read according to me.

Title: Tomb of Sand
Author: Geetanjali Shree
My Review:
_Tomb of Sand_

Tomb of Sand is Daisy Rockwell's translation of Geetanjali Shree's 2018 novel रेत समाधि (Ret Samadhi). The first Hindi translated work to win a booker prize, it follows the matriarch of a family ‘Ma’ from her depression after her husband’s death to her life thereafter: moving in with her daughter (‘Beti’) from elder son’s (‘Bade’) house and her friendship with Rosie: a transgender person. As they say in the book “At eighty, Ma had turned selfish.”

A deeply layered book, the translation is a job well done. There are Urdu, Hindi, Punjabi and Sanskrit references to poetry, songs, literature and movies that are kept as such. The book rightly captures the polyphonous Indian family where no language is spoken un-adulterated. Spoken Hindi is peppered with English words. Such linguistic hybridity is difficult to capture in writing. You can feel the Hindi peeking at you behind the English translation. But as Daisy rightly says, if the English feels as if it’s thinly veiling the Hindi phrases to you as a Hindi speaker, then you could simply read the original.

The book goes at a very slow pace like meandering rambles of a family. In a way the writing is remarkable and unconventional. She writes as if there is no boundary, as if there is no hurry. ‘Ma’ can take as long as she likes to reveal her ways to us. It’s as if the book is asking us to take a break if we want to, but the protagonist ‘Ma’ won’t. You are welcome to walk with her or if you are annoyed you are most welcome to wait while Ma does her things.
That kind of a feel as if ‘Ma’ is challenging you is felt throughout the book and to me felt like a refreshing device to invite the reader to the protagonist’s life although reading a work driven by language and not plot can be quite challenging.

The mother-daughter relationship is beautifully captured and Gitanjali Shree has wonderfully brought out the small Indian family dynamics. By referring to characters as nouns and not names, she brings to life the roles of people in that household, the layers hiding beneath each roles, in effect giving a sensory experience of an Indian life.

It was certainly not a breezy beach read for me as was described by booker prize judges. The book does not blow you away, but it evokes nostalgia and candid introspection.

Title: Neanderthal Man: In Search of Lost Genomes
Author: Svante Pääbo
My Review:
_Neanderthal Man_

“Where do we humans come from, and how are we related to extinct hominins? “
Svante Paabo was awarded the 2022 Nobel Prize in Medicine for his discoveries concerning genomes of Neanderthal and human evolution. A scientific book written by Paabo himself in part memoir style explains his life’s work starting from his graduate student days in 1980s.

Paabo introduces us to biological and technical details about extracting genomes from ancient bones, about Neanderthals, their relationship and contributions to modern humans and much more. Most importantly he discovered the flow of genes from extinct archaic humans like Neanderthals to present-day humans and it’s physiological relevance today.

Reading it is like listening to Paabo speak to you over dinner, taking us in his decades long journey as a researcher.
Paabo writes unabashedly of what it is to be a PhD student, a post-grad, supervisor/project lead and mentor to his students.
Paabo walks you through life in the lab: the Friday meetings, the publication process, starting and ending collaborations, acquiring funding and life in general as a researcher.

Having chosen research as a career myself, it was wonderful to hear Paabo talk about his research, the sheer commitment that goes into it, pure joy of discovery and ofcourse the equally terrifying sinking feeling when things don’t open up to you.

If you want to know about human evolution and what life as a researcher involves on an everyday basis, then this book is riveting.

Title: Krishnakanta's Will
Author: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
My Review:
_Krishnakanta’s Will_

Bankim Chandra Chatterjee was one of the most important novelist of 19th century India and the composer of ‘Vande Mataram’, the national song of India. Published in 1878, the book was originally written in Bengali and translated to English by J.C Ghosh.

While it’s a typical story of family drama involving forged wills and extra marital affairs set in the background of social conventions of that time, it paints a vivid picture of 19th century social practices of India, particularly Bengal, which at that period was undergoing social reforms in the form of liberalization of the strict orthodoxy of the Hindu elite. In particular the book is written in the context of liberalisations in Hindu widow remarriages.

Contrary to popular opinion, I did not feel that the author was taking the side of characters who went against accepted social morals, rather I thought the whole work is simply an exposition of the then accepted social morals. Bankim Chandra Chatterjee does not go for a detailed fleshing out of the characters, further cementing the idea that the book is very simply an overview of what life was like for an elite Hindu Woman in 19th century Bengal.

The book is not a work that may thrill the readers of today, nevertheless I found it very illuminating.

Title: In Light of India
Author: Octavio Paz
My Review:
_In Light Of India_

In Light of India is the Mexican poet and the 1990 Nobel Prize laureate, Octavio Paz’s ‘reflections, impressions and objections that India provoked in him’ during his stay as Mexico’s Ambassador to India in the years following India’s independence. Originally written in Spanish, it was translated to English by #eliotweinberger.

Paz’s writing is elegant, lyrical and intimate. He ruminates deeply about India’s religious identities, Sanskrit poetry, art, paintings, philosophy, the birth of the idea of India as a Nation, Gandhi, Nehru, Savarkar, the difference in their ideologies and their visions of India as a nation. He further talks about the ideological beginning of Hindu Nationalist Movements, its doctrines and the subsequent birth of Bharatiya Janata Party.

“…Its idea of Indian culture is religious; its vision of the Hindu religion entails its transformation into a political belief. The conversion of a culture into a religion ends with the conversion of a religion into politics.
…. That is, a political corruption of religion. In the Islamic tradition this confusion has been recurrent and one of the negative aspects of the history of Arab civilisation”

His reflections and insights on the Indian scriptures, Bhagavat-Gita, caste system and the centuries long coexistence of Islam and Hinduism in India are thought-provoking. He also explores similarities and differences between Mexico and India in terms of their culture, cuisine, shared history of colonisation and its profound influence on their identities.
Interestingly, he also ruminates on the concept of Time as seen by the various religions of India and contribution of such synthesis of Time to India’s Identity.

Paz writes passionately, like a man in love. A short wonderful read for anyone interested to explore the abstract boundaries of India.

Title: The Argumentative Indian: Writings on Indian History, Culture and Identity
Author: Amartya Sen
My Review:
_The Argumentative Indian_

“While we cannot live without history, we cannot live within it either” #Amartyasen

Through a collection of well connected essays, the economist and Nobel laureate celebrates the long history of argumentative and reasoning tradition in India which formed the root of our democracy.

Dr. Sen looks back to this tradition and celebration of heterodoxy in India from Emperor Ashoka to Mughal Emperor Akbar and their state sponsored reasoning based approach inviting all religion and even atheistic groups to arrive at a solution backed by reason rather than blind faith.
Dr. Sen also illustrates this practice in modern day using relationship of Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore who despite contradictory viewpoints of nationalism, patriotism and many more shared a deep respect for each other.

He devotes chapters to explain the unique concept and nature of secularism, what it means to be secular in India and how the constitution and the institutions work to implement the same. He goes on to warn about the Hindutva Nationalist movements, it’s repercussions and how such intolerant ideologies threaten India’s pluralism and secularism.

Dr. Sen also devotes chapters to statistically backed discussions on gender, caste and economic inequality, it’s interrelationships and the power of education. He concludes with a very interesting discussion of identity and his views on a choice based identity rather than identity as a discovery. As he rightly says ‘the identity of an individual is essentially a function of their choices, rather than the discovery of an immutable attribute’.

Unlike contemporary books on India, Amartya Sen’s book is a scholarly book with excellent references, citations and footnotes making it open for any reader to verify, contemplate and introspect his ideas, his visions and his notes on history.

It is a book that does not trivialise India’s pluralism but goes on to illustrate the complexity behind it. A book I’m sure to read again and again in my lifetime

Title: The Blind Assassin
Author: Margaret Atwood
My Review:
_The Blind Assassin_

“If you knew what was going to happen, if you knew everything that was going to happen next—if you knew in advance the consequences of your own actions—you'd be doomed. You'd be ruined as God. You'd be a stone. You'd never eat or drink or laugh or get out of bed in the morning. You'd never love anyone, ever again. You'd never dare to..” #margaretatwood

A booker prize winning book by #margaretatwood, #theblindassassin is a complex story of two siblings belonging to a once rich Chase family set in 20th century Canada during the world war times.

The narrative is complex. It uses more than an unreliable protagonist to move the story forward. Iris begins the story with the compelling sentence, “10 days after the war ended, my sister Laura drove off a car of the bridge”.

In addition to Iris’s writings, we are provided with news paper articles and letters relating to the Chase Family to objectively look at the incidents. Also the narrative is interspersed with extracts from a novel (a novel within a novel) about a conservative rich woman and a man on the run, in a risky affair telling sci-fi stories to each other during their clandestine meet-ups, seemingly written by Laura Chase and published posthumously by her sister and protagonist Iris Chase.

All these narrative strands meet up to give a satisfying if not an altogether surprising end to the history of Chase Family.
Iris’s account do occasionally begin to get tedious, but it is a reflection of Iris’s character. Her wry observations remind us that it’s not a simple memoir as you would expect, but a much more complex attempt to redeem her past and offer a remorseless testament to her sister and what remains of her family.

Blind Assassin is not a quick read and may frustrate readers to move with Iris chase as she battles old age and rambles on about her life and of her sister’s. I found it a multi-layered and complex read much like Ishiguro’s ‘Remains of the Day’ minus the melancholic revelation. Iris is more blunt and accepting of her life choices than Steven.

Title: Blindness
Author: José Saramago
My Review:
_Blindness_

“This is the stuff we're made of, half indifference, half malice “ #josesaramago

Blindness is an unsettling book by Portuguese writer Josè Saramago who won the Nobel prize of literature in 1998.

A philosophical speculative fiction involving a mysterious blindness epidemic where people suddenly go blind and the blindness spreads. The government panics and rounds up all the blind people to put them in unsupervised, under-provisioned quarantine. Saramago writes about how loss of just one sense causes people to live in unimaginable filth and nauseating atmosphere, a city reduced to savagery.

Translated from Portuguese by Giovanni Pontiero, the plot line felt like Philip Zimbarbo’s Stanford Prison experiment stretched to a ‘what if’ scenario with excruciating details.

The writing is without any nouns or punctuations and involves unparagraphed dialogues making it a difficult and slow read. The writing perhaps conveys
confusion in which a world of blind
people may exist causing us to be equally frustrated and helpless as a reader. It was impossible to read it as a third person. Every time you open the book you are one of the blind and Saramago makes you feel claustrophobic and disturbed. All the more reason why the book has to be closed down every now and then.

It is doubtless an excellent work but reading it was a challenge both in prose and content. Numerous times I wanted to put down the book but I suppose it has to be read slowly and in intervals. It is a memorable book but not one I would want to read again or recommend without inhibitions.

Title: Klara and the Sun
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
_Klara and the Sun_

“Until recently, I didn’t think that humans could choose
loneliness. That there were sometimes forces more powerful than the wish to avoid loneliness.” #kazuoishiguro

A dystopian speculative fiction, Ishiguro introduces us to Klara, an AF (Artificial Friend) bought by a family for their teenage daughter Josie. They are lonely because in Josie’s world, kids don’t go to school but study at home through screen tutors. Typical of his style, there are only subtle hints to the shape of future the story is set in, leaving the details to the imagination of reader.

We are shown the near future through the observations of Klara. From the bits we are shown through Klara, it is understood that privileged people choose to genetically modify their children or to have them ‘lifted’ to provide better life prospects in a deeply meritocratic society. But ‘lifting’ has its risks, sometimes causing unnamed illnesses that lead to death. What we encounter is a society at the edge of transition, thus causing deep divides in search for perfection in progeny and discrimination among ‘lifted’ and ‘un-lifted’

The Ishiguro artistic perfection is less here compared to his ‘Remains of the Day’ or ‘Never Let Me Go’. No moment struck my chord like when Stevens reflects on his memories in ‘Remains of the Day’. Perhaps it is meant to be that way as a subtle reminder to Klara’s machine-ness. Klara’s empathy and spirituality does not persuade us of her humanness but makes you reflect if humans acquire feelings similarly as her. As Klara says, “I believe I have many feelings,”. “The more I observe, the more feelings become available to me.”

Though not Ishiguro’s best work, it was an elonquent read with a fresh look at the fragility of humanity.
