Title: The Handmaid’s Tale (The Handmaid's Tale, #1)
Author: Margaret Atwood
My Review:
_The Handmaid’s Tale_

“Maybe it isn't really about who can own whom, who can do what to whom and get away with it, even as far as death. Maybe it isn't about who can sit and who has to kneel or stand or lie down, legs spread open. Maybe it's about who can do what to whom and be forgiven for it. Never tell me it amounts to the same thing” #handmaidstale

#margaretatwood describes a dystopian United States which has been transformed via a military coup to a totalitarian theocracy ‘Republic of Gilead’. In this society, roles of woman are reduced to those assigned from their interpretation of Old Testament. Banned from reading and writing, owning property or handling finances, a woman is to only be an empty vessel whose social status elevates only if they successfully create a progeny for the man.

In the social hierarchy women can only be the Wives, domestic helps (the Marthas), sex workers (the Jezebels), female Teachers/guards (the Aunts) who ‘train’ young girls for their roles to be performed, wombs (the Handmaids), or, if they are unsuited for any of these roles, Unwomen who are sent off to be labourers either assigned to farms if lucky or to clean out radioactive waste if they aren't.

Of these, the protagonist Offred is a Handmaid, they being a communal property moved from house to house to be inseminated by men of power under the supervision of their wives.

Unlike other #dystopianfiction, we do not directly plunge into the conditions of society. A unique element here is how the protagonist’s constant reminiscing offers the reader a look at how the regime change came to be. The steps, the protests and before you know it, you are hunted for being an ‘Unwoman’.

The book is written as a transcript of personal recordings by Offred collected by historians during what later came to be knows as the ‘Gilead Era’. So while it’s short and mostly easy to read, the structure and lack of any indication when the protagonist shifts from past to present may sometimes slow your progress. I found the book very engaging and as a warning to what future may hold.

Title: The Andromeda Strain (Andromeda, #1)
Author: Michael Crichton
My Review:
_The Andromeda Strain_

“scientific research was much like prospecting: you went out and you hunted, armed with your maps and your instruments, but in the end your preparations did not matter, or even your intuition. You needed your luck, and whatever benefits accrued to the diligent, through sheer, grinding hard work.” #michaelcrichton

Michael Crichton’s ‘Jurassic Park’ series, ‘Congo’ and ‘Micro’ were my first introductions to sci-fi 14 years ago. His books are always scientifically compelling, fast paced and thrilling. Andromeda Strain is once again a well executed and detail oriented science fiction.

A man made-satellite crash lands in a desolate area of Arizona. The team deployed to recover the satellite loses contact abruptly. An aerial view witnesses all the inhabitants littered around few miles of crash site presumably dead except for an old man and a baby.

The satellite suspected to carry an unidentified dangerous contaminant leads the project team to quickly activate ‘Wildfire’ a protocol that brings in 5 biologists/scientists to isolate, study, characterise and contain threats of this nature.

The 1969 book is written like a documentary. We see the steps taken to characterise the microorganism. The discussions thereafter and the next steps taken are research oriented and scientifically detailed. Despite that it is well written and although an unpopular opinion, I thought the ending was well done. It felt like a logical conclusion to the train of technical discussions.

PS: At this point, biological super spreader events do not feel like fiction.

Title: The Calcutta Chromosome
Author: Amitav Ghosh
My Review:
_The Calcutta Chromosome_

Amitav Ghosh’s book is a speculative sci-fi based on the life of Ronald Ross, whose breakthrough research on malaria in 1989 won him the Nobel Prize.

Starting from investigating the discrepancies in Ross’s malaria research, the steps of Ross' discovery are shown as remarkably fortuitous, and this is where the author focuses his attention. Ghosh attempts to recreate the story of Ross’s discovery of the malarial parasite. Apart from the fact that Ross discovered the malarial parasite on 20th August, 1897; all the other events in the book are fabricated by the author which won him the Arthur C Clarke Award in 1997.

Amitav Ghosh introduces some clever ideas filling in these discrepancies with what he terms as an ongoing secret non-traditional research on Calcutta chromosome, an unusual chromosome that may not be isolated or detected by conventional techniques. The author speculates that such a chromosome may be developed from a process of recombination which is particular to every individual and is perhaps responsible for individual traits. It cannot not be transferred from one generation to another. It is only present in the non regenerative tissue, in other words; the brain and perhaps can be transmitted through malaria creating a potential of transferring individual traits from one host to another.

While I enjoyed the discussions on the interesting possibilities of human consciousness transferability, the book ends open ended and is left to the readers’ interpretation. That and the confusing multi-timeline writing style may not be to everybody’s taste.

Title: Haroun and the Sea of Stories (Khalifa Brothers, #1)
Author: Salman Rushdie

Title: The Assassination of Rajiv Gandhi
Author: Neena Gopal
My Review:
_The Assassination Of Rajiv Gandhi_

On 21st May, 1991, Neena Gopal was interviewing Rajiv Gandhi during the election rally at Sriperumbudur, Tamil Nadu. Gandhi’s ‘Z’ security cover had been withdrawn by the V.P. Singh government, and only his lone bodyguard was present with him on the day. Neena Gopal asked him if he feared for his life.

In response, #rajivgandhi asked: “Have you noticed how every time a South Asian leader rises to a position of power or is about to achieve something, he is cut down, attacked, killed...”

Moments later, Rajiv Gandhi was assassinated by a suicide bomber along with 14 others. #neenagopal became the last journalist to have interviewed Gandhi. In her book, she reconstructs the chain of events that led to this day, from the political climate in India and Sri Lanka, involvement of India in Sri Lankan civil war, removal of ‘Z’ security cover for Gandhi, ignored warnings from intelligence agencies an year back that hinted at a possible attack, the hatching of plan in LTTE headquarters in Sri Lanka and everything that led to the assassination of a wonderful man who was at the brink of a second term as Prime Minister of the largest democracy in the world and whose death became a tremendous loss for India.

Rajiv Gandhi stepping in as the youngest PM of India after the assassination of his mother and then PM Indira Gandhi, was the first step to a paradigm shift in Indian politics. His decision to send Indian Peace Keeping Forces (IPKF) to Sri Lanka to end civil war and help create a state that is inclusive of Sri lankan Tamils came at the cost of his life.
LTTE leader V. Prabhakaran saw this peace keeping strategy as treachery and an attempt to quash LTTE’s dreams of a separate Tamil state. This led to the harbouring of a deep hatred for Rajiv Gandhi and LTTE saw his rise to a second term as PM as a threat to their existence.

A well paced book with good background work and information provided about 1980’s India and Sri Lanka political climate and it’s repercussions.

Title: The Sound of Things Falling
Author: Juan Gabriel Vásquez
My Review:
“Adulthood brings with it the pernicious illusion of control, and perhaps even depends on it. I mean that mirage of dominion over our own life that allows us to feel like adults, for we associate maturity with autonomy, the sovereign right to determine what is going to happen to us next. Disillusion comes sooner or later, but it always comes, it doesn’t miss an appointment, it never has.” #JuanGabrielVásquez

Originally written in Spanish, this Latin American literature was translated to English by Anne Mclean, the work delves into the political landscape of Colombia especially it’s history of drug trafficking.
The protagonist belongs to the generation of people who were raised amidst the war between drug kingpins and government forces of the 1960’s, Bogota, Columbia.
A time when drug lords such as the legendary cocaine king Pablo Escobar (known as the wealthiest criminal in history, single handedly started and ran the drug cartel) ran the country.

In such a time, the protagonist is accidentally shot and his friend murdered by random people. The story follows the protagonist transformation after the event. He lives in the aftermath, unable to move forward and able to relate only with people who were directly affected by the incident. He spends his time discovering his murdered friend’s life and the way his life too was shaped by his country’s violent history.

The background is beautifully painted. The protagonist perspectives becomes harder to relate to towards the end, perhaps because that kind of a life can only be lived and experienced. Perhaps also because the protagonist is introduced as a boring person and his life after the incident changes too much for such a simple man to handle and perhaps for the reader to relate beyond a point.

I found the part of his murdered friend Ricardo and his family’s stories very consuming. Through these stories, Vasquez confronts the history of his country Colombia in an engaging and well paced writing.

Title: Harry Potter and the Cursed Child: Parts One and Two (Harry Potter, #8)
Author: J.K. Rowling

Title: Good Omens: The Nice and Accurate Prophecies of Agnes Nutter, Witch
Author: Terry Pratchett
My Review:
Angel Aziraphale and demon Crowley are the earthly representatives of Good and Evil. Over the years, Crowley and Aziraphale have become fond of each other and are also not too keen for the approaching apocalypse. They have acquired a certain taste for earthly life which they find it hard to let go and live what they deem a rather tasteless life in Heaven or Hell.

As the apocalypse approaches 10 years later, they realise that the anti-christ has been misplaced. Instead of sending the baby off with satanic nuns, the baby was accidentally switched to a seemingly boring suburban family.

The first half of the book with Aziraphale, Crowley and their discussions to avert the dooms day were rather good. But the latter part of the book was a dry spell for me. There were lots of characters introduced lacking motive or character arcs and the kid’s interactions were not very engaging. I took a lot more time to read than I anticipated because at some point I lost the motivation and almost decided to leave it unfinished.

The interesting bits about the book is the premise and way they satirically discuss free will, Good, Evil and what indeed was God thinking ? Perhaps this thread explored is the amusing thing about the book.

Title: One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest
Author: Ken Kesey

Title: The Color Purple
Author: Alice Walker
My Review:
“I'm pore, I'm black, I may be ugly and can't cook, a voice say to everything listening. But I'm here.” #alicewalker

The color purple is a discovery of the origin of identity and voice when you are taught to have none.

The book is a moving story about two African-American sisters Celie and Nettie living in the early 20th century America, separated by circumstances. Through a series of letters, first from Celie to God and then the sisters to each other, we take a journey from their dark, gritty invisible youth to their strong, resilient and beautifully content adulthood.

The character development purely through letters is splendidly done and weaves one of the most powerful stories I have read.

PS: “I think it pisses God off if you walk by the color purple in a field somewhere and don't notice it. People think pleasing God is all God cares about. But any fool living in the world can see it always trying to please us back.”

Title: A Game of Thrones (A Song of Ice and Fire, #1)
Author: George R.R. Martin

Title: The Hobbit
Author: Chuck Dixon
Additional Authors: David Wenzel, Sean Deming, J.R.R. Tolkien

Title: Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix (Harry Potter, #5, Part 1)
Author: J.K. Rowling

Title: The Hindu Way: An Introduction to Hinduism
Author: Shashi Tharoor

Title: The Palace of Illusions
Author: Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni
My Review:
“Because ultimately only the witness and not the actors knows the truth (Vyasa to Draupadi)”

Narrated by Draupadi, the wife of the Pandavas, ‘The Palace Of Illusions’ is the retelling of the epic ‘Mahabharata’ from the point of view of Draupadi.

From her birth, to her lonely childhood with her patriarchal father and beloved brother, to her complicated marriage to 5 husbands, to her cold relationship with her mother-in-law Kunti and of-course her charming friendship with Krishna, the book explores her unconscious feelings that mark her historic presence.

And no, Draupadi was never the pious woman like Gandhari or like the single minded Kunti, but a raw, fierce, haughty, intelligent woman with a scathing tongue who demanded respect and considered herself as equal as her husband’s and probably more.

It is the retelling of the events and most importantly the responses to those events that led to the Great War of Kurukshetra.

The author also takes the liberty to explore the relationship between Karna and Draupadi, which I found fascinating.

Those of you who have not read Mahabharata, the book offers a grandiose glimpse into it and those like me who have read it, loved it, whose entire childhood was sprinkled with stories from Mahabharata and Ramayana, the book offers a unique perspective and gentleness that perhaps only Draupadi can provide.

I forgot how much insightful, thrilling and hauntingly accurate Mahabharata was. I’m forever awed by it’s logical strategies, counselling and depiction of human rawnesses. It was pure pleasure to read and visit the characters again!

Title: Interpreter of Maladies
Author: Jhumpa Lahiri
My Review:
“You got cats at home?"
No cats. Only a husband” #jhumpalahiri

Lahiri’s words effortlessly create the stories that human beings cling on desperately, to give meaning to their lives as circumstances change. Her stories are intimate and real.
All I can do is smile and hope that it conveys all the subtleties that her stories encapsulate.

Title: Bhima Lone Warrior
Author: എം.ടി. വാസുദേവന്‍നായര്‍ | M.T.Vasudevan Nair
My Review:
_Bhima, The Lone Warrior_

Or tilted ‘Randamoozham’ in original Malayalam version. Written by MT Vasudevan (or M.T. as he is known to us Malayalees) The book is Mahabharata from the eyes of Bhima, the second of the Pandavas.

The translation is wonderfully done and the book is a masterpiece by the Jnanpith winning writer. So much more research and thought has went into it.

As MT says, his work was inspired from the many pregnant pauses in the original epic, motivating him to fill those silences.

He strips the characters of their divinity and presents them as mere mortals of flesh, blood and desires. We have Krishna, the mediator, the counsellor, undivine, human and raw. You love his words and resent his words. You feel the unjustness and justness of it. You feel the human need to win.

MT goes on to strip the divinity of parenthood we have so often read in these stories of Pandavas and says that his research has led him to conclude these as mostly imaginations of the story tellers.

Many acute observations are sharply made by the author making it a wonderful read.

I can read as many renditions of Mahabharata as possible and never be bored.

Title: The Forest of Enchantments
Author: Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni
My Review:
“If you want to stand up against wrongdoing, if you want to bring about change, do it in a way that doesn’t bruise a man’s pride. You’ll have a better chance of success.” #chitra

Chitra divakaruni’s book is a retelling of Ramayan from the perspective of Sita.
The Sita here is not portrayed as fierce and outspoken simply for the sake of portraying a strong woman, instead Sita is the Sita we have come to know, ever graceful, ever patient but sharp and resilient, a queen fit to rule a kingdom.

The art of making a home, simple compassion, perseverance, patience and kindness, those qualities that we consider mundane and largely associate with feminine weakness shows it’s permeance and importance in running and raising a home and a Kingdom.

It is also the story of other misunderstood women in the epic: Koushalya, Kaikeyi, Surpanakha, Mandodari, Sarama, Ahalya etc which makes it an interesting read.

The men in the story are not to be hated. Over the years we have questioned and hated Ram’s ethics but this retelling gently peels to reveal Ram’s anguish and fear of becoming his father who destroyed the kingdom simply by prioritising his wife. Therefore in his obsessive need to purely satisfy each and every common man, he chooses to sacrifice his wife over and over again.

The book is a simple read with gentle pace. But the writing style is mediocre with poor prose and certain sections feeling dragged and unkempt. But other periphery characters, their insights and observations make it an overall illuminating read.

PS: I was largely able to ignore the unattractive prose due to my love for Indian epics, probably may test the patience of another reader.

Title: Where the Rain is Born: Writings About Kerala
Author: Anita Nair
My Review:
“Nowhere else in the world have I seen so many hues of green. The velvety green of the moss on the wall. The deep green of the hibiscus bush. The dappled green of the jackfruit. The jade green of the paddy leaves. Parakeets wings. Tree frogs. The opaque green of silence.” #anitanair


The book is a collection of short stories and poems with Kerala as it’s backdrop.

Reading it was like sitting on a rainy day in a ‘nadan thattukada’ (local tea-shop) with our hot ‘chaya’ (tea) having a soft ‘Puttu’ (steam cake?) and ‘Meen curry’ (spicy fish curry) possibly with a sweet ‘cherupazham’ (a variety of banana), (On another note, nowhere else I have seen so many varieties of banana !)
and watching the very many hues of green that spread across your views.

There are stories from evergreen Malayalam writers like MT Vasudevan Nair, OV Vijayan, Thakazhi Sivasankara Pillai and also voices of contemporary writers like Arundhati Roy, Shashi Tharoor etc.
They bring to light both the extremes of this beautiful state, taking apart the nostalgia and attempting to see Kerala for what it truly is holding to contrast the high literacy rate and the stifling conservative attitudes of the average Malayali.

Kerala is my home and monsoon in Kerala is a poetry by itself 🌧.
So if you want to glimpse into the lives of an average Keralite from the past to the present and feel the monsoon and the green and the people, this is the book you want to read.

PS: My favourites were ‘Karkitakam’ by MT Vasudevan, ‘The blue light’ by Vaikom Muhammad Basheer and ‘Charlis and I’ by Shashi Tharoor.

Title: A Man Called Ove
Author: Fredrik Backman
My Review:
“It's a strange thing, becoming an orphan at sixteen. To lose your family long before you've had time to create your own to replace it. It's a very specific sort of loneliness…” #fredrikbackman

A sweet sweet story by Fredrik Backman, reading it was like feeling cotton candy melt in your mouth as you close your eyes and walk amongst a crowd.

We are introduced to a man called Ove, who comes across as an unpleasant man. As we watch his daily routine, we are also told simultaneously what made the man Ove, his life with Sonja, his principles, discipline and devotion to his work and to his life in general.

And as you read, you melt. And that’s the only thing you can do. Melt slowly like a candle as you learn about the man called Ove.

Title: The Lucifer Effect: Understanding How Good People Turn Evil
Author: Philip G. Zimbardo
My Review:
“Any deed that any human being has ever committed, however horrible is possible for any of us-under the right or wrong situational circumstances. That knowledge does not excuse evil; rather it democratises it, sharing its blame among ordinary actors rather than declaring it the province only of deviants and despots-of Them but not Us. “ #philipzimbarbo

In the summer of 1971, a landmark study was conducted in which a group of college-student volunteers were randomly given the roles of “guards” and “prisoners” and then placed in a mock prison environment in Stanford University.
The study had to be abandoned just after 6 days as the volunteers transformed into either brutal guards or emotionally broken prisoners.

The experiment was conducted to observe if and how situations or a system can cause behavioural transformation of people, it’s transiency and nature.

Philip Zimbarbo provides an in-depth analysis of his classic experiment and takes as case study different crimes against humanity over the years including horrific abuses in Abu Ghraib and Guantanamo prisons, genocide of Tutsi community in Rwanda, of Jews by Nazi regime to name a few.

While underlining the weight of situational factors on individual behaviours, Zimbarbo makes it a point to note that understanding the why of what was done, does not excuse what was done. ‘Psychological analysis is not excusology’

The book although written in simple English, is a discussion of research conducted, hence it is intense and requires strong attention. My general interest in social psychology led me to this work (Let me know if you have read it! ).

PS: A parallel to this study conducted ten years earlier was Stanley Milgram’s Obedience to Authority which showed how regular people can very easily be made to obey a heinous order.

Both these studies show the effect and importance of the power hierarchy in systems and how very easily we can dehumanise a person or community and lead an entire nation to commit atrocities.
For full details of the experiment and it’s analysis, read #obediencetoauthority by #stanleymilgram

Title: One Part Woman
Author: Perumal Murugan
My Review:
_One Part Woman_

“The wretched people around us do not see what a man has. They only see what a man doesn't have.” #perumalmurugan

Kali and Ponna are happily married couple. Childless for 12 years, they face intense ridicule, taunting and isolation from the rest of their village community.

There is an annual festival honouring a half male-half female deity, during which consensual sex between any man and woman is celebrated. The book explores the extent to which the couple is pushed and abused by the society to conceive.

Set in the backdrop of colonial era in rural Tamil Nadu in Southern India, the book (originally in Tamil language) boldly explores casteism, societal pressure, infertility, rituals, traditions and the effect these have on relationships and individuals.

Although the translation sometimes feels discontinuous, it is still an engaging read.
The energy of the village life and sharpness of the society is captured well enough.

Apparently the book generated a huge controversy for its depiction of religion, caste and sex, with copies of books burnt by certain factions till Madras High Court ruled in favour of the author’s rights.

Title: The Cake Tree in the Ruins
Author: Akiyuki Nosaka
My Review:
“I’m still unable to leave the burnt-out ruins” #akiyukinosaka


A collection of short stories by Akiyuki Nosaka, translated by Ginny Tapley Takemori, set just before 15, August 1945 when Japan surrendered to the Allies marking the end of WW 2.

Nosaka was part of the the ‘yakeato’ generation, ‘the generation of the ashes’ who survived the fire bombing of their country during the second world war.

Nosaka lost his parents to the war and his little sister died shortly afterwords due to malnutrition. The 12 powerful tales in this book are inspired from his memories of that time.

The stories with a touch of magical realism, fantasy and child like innocence are told from the perspective of pet parrots, wolf, whales etc. They bring to light the brutality of war and what it leaves behind for the people.

PS: Nosaka’s most popular work is perhaps ‘Grave of the Fireflies’ which is based on his personal experience of trying to save his little sister from malnutrition. This collection does not include that title

Title: The Secret History
Author: Donna Tartt
My Review:
“There is nothing wrong with the love of Beauty. But Beauty - unless she is wed to something more meaningful - is always superficial.” #donnatartt

Donna Tart’s debut work can be succinctly summarised as a modern day Greek tragedy.

| Synopsis |
The story is about 6 impressionable, prodigious students who learn Ancient Greek in college under the tutelage of Julian Marrow who is very selective of his students and insists on near total isolation of the group from other faculties and student groups.
The story begins with the unreliable narration by Richard, of the events that led to the murder of one among them.

| Observations |
The professor though friendly and passionate, sets a heavy atmosphere for the students bringing out a sense of perfectionism and grey morality that percolates into all of them and instills in them a need to shed ‘normalcy’ and become free of constrained self.

At a single glance, you do not see the professors shadow in what the students ended up doing. In fact the whole of book has barely few interactions shown with the professor.

I felt the professor’s ideas captivating and I could see how it enthrals a group of vulnerable, slightly misfit group of passionate students.
It is my understanding that any idea expressed in a closed room, closed group set-up can make the talks feel like a secret to life that the lesser beings do not know, one which the select few have been shown. While the setup can feel insignificant to outsiders, the impact of this is quite heavy on the listeners. The book explores this concept beautifully and subtly.

| Writing Style |
The plot is easy to follow and language is much easier compared to ‘A Little Friend’ but still not an easy read.
The writing is well done and sets a grim, grand atmosphere quite resonating to that of Ancient Greek tales of tragic grandiose.

PS: I felt the book explores how assimilating grand ideas and thoughts without first observing or sharing their flow or at least anchoring your sense of self before letting them take full control can lead to quite significant consequences.

Title: Midnight in Chernobyl: The Untold Story of the World's Greatest Nuclear Disaster
Author: Adam Higginbotham
My Review:
|A Brief Look|
On 25 April 1986, a routine maintenance test was scheduled in reactor number 4 of Chernobyl. The test was intended to check a key safety system designed to protect the reactor during an electrical blackout.

25 year old engineer incharge Leonid Toptunov began to power down the reactor. Soon after, a lot of things happen quickly. Reactor core reached 4,650 degrees Celsius; the surface of the sun is 5,500. At 1:24 am, a catastrophic explosion tears apart reactor number 4. The core of the reactor was completely destroyed.

KGB cut down phone lines and seals of the city so that no news of the incident reaches the outer world. No one was allowed to leave. It took two days before an order was given to move the 50,000 inhabitants out of Pripyat, the city built next to the plant.

USSR downplayed the crisis, alarmed at losing face before the international community. On 28th April, radiation levels were detected in Sweden and Finland. It was Sweden’s search for the source of radioactivity after they concluded it wasn’t from their plant, that hinted at a major mishap in the Soviet.

It is considered the worst nuclear disaster in history both in cost and casualties.
The technical solutions or the financial means to manage a disaster like this was beyond humankind.

| About the Book|
The author, reveals in dense details, the events starting from the cover ups surrounding the previous RBMK accidents, the decade long suppressed warnings of of the flawed reactor design and the way it’s operators were misled about its behaviour.
Piece by piece the author reconstructs the events of the fateful night, the attempted cover up of it and the events that contributed to the disaster due to decades of secrecy, propaganda, misinformation, bureaucracy and a blindly fearful obedience to party.
Mishandling of Chernobyl would turn out to be the crucial factor in the collapse of USSR.

The book is wonderfully written with engaging technical and political details. I highly recommend it, a one of a kind historical investigation.

Title: Samskara: A Rite for a Dead Man
Author: U.R. Ananthamurthy
My Review:
_Samskara_

In the Agraharam, a Brahmin has died. But all the others hesitate to perform the cremation rites for he was the one who for years had defied all rules of Brahminism with his acts of eating meat, drinking alcohol and living with a lower caste woman.

The community approaches Praneshacharya, the learnt man of vedas and the unofficial head of this Brahmin community to decide how to and who should cremate the body. Praneshcharya with all his learning fails to rise up to the occasion and provide a solution. The death of this man causes moral dilemma and conflict in Praneshcharya which all his learning cannot satiate.

First published in 1965, and translated from Kannada by AK Ramanujan, the book encapsulates the ideologies, theology and lays bare the hypocrisy of the Brahmin society of that time.

A controversial book at the time, the writer questions the relevance of belief system and practices which cannot solve practical problems.

PS: A wonderful read. It makes me want to learn Kannada just so I can read the original version.

Title: Train to Pakistan
Author: Khushwant Singh
My Review:
“Freedom is for the educated people who fought for it. We were slaves of the English, now we will be slaves of the educated Indians—or the Pakistanis.” #khushwanthsingh

It is 1947. The time of partition between India and Pakistan. There is daily news about conflicts, killings and corpses arriving on trains. Mano Majra, a fictional village in the border is not yet tainted by this erupting violence.

Here, a small community of Sikhs and Muslims live peacefully. Soon Mano Majra is tested. Their patience, logic, reason and love stretched by characters in authority.

Khushwant Singh, shows the role, impact and ease of each character in aiding and abetting communal violence. The simplicity of inciting violence based on religion and also the simplicity of avoiding it are portrayed in this short intense read.

Train to Pakistan is about common people who are made to feel helpless, it’s about government officials who know things, watch things and refuse to act or take responsibility, it’s about educated youth who think too much but fail to provide solutions. It is an account of the 1940’s India where, though we were independent, there was deep unrest spreading throughout.

Khushwant Singh talks about religious extremism, humanness, empathy, and fickleness of mind in a common man and manipulations by those in power to be in power. He discusses the seemingly simple interactions that leads to communal violence keeping alive the empathy instead of treating the partition like another statistic.

With each page, a remorse builds up in you because though the book is set in 1940’s, the reality in the present is eerily similar. It is 2022 and we are still intolerant, confused and can be easily riled up in the name of religion.

PS: “Morality is a matter of money. Poor people cannot afford to have morals. So they have religion”

Title: The Spy and the Traitor: The Greatest Espionage Story of the Cold War
Author: Ben Macintyre
My Review:
“It is perfectly possible for two people to listen to the same words and hear entirely different things” #benmacyntire

In 1985, a KGB colonel appeared in front of a bakery holding a plastic bag from Supermarket ‘Safeway’. Also passing the road was a MI6 intelligence agent wearing grey trousers eating a ‘mars’ bar and holding a Harrods bag.
This was the signal to activate ‘Operation Pimlico’ to exfiltrate the KGB double agent from the Soviet territory.

This is a true story of Oleg Gordievsky, a KGB spy turned MI6 (British intelligence agency) informant. Disillusioned with USSR propaganda and ideologies, Oleg turned a double agent and started working for MI6 for 11 years undetected.

Oleg Gordeivsky’s actions and contributions are considered invaluable at the key juncture of Cold War in understanding the Kremlin way of thinking and possibly playing a major role in avoiding a nuclear war between NATO and USSR at the peak of Cold War. His insights are considered to have changed the course of Cold War.

His extradition from USSR was considered one of the most stunning feat achieved considering that the KGB (Committee for State Security, USSR) at its height during the Cold War, was the world’s largest secret police and intelligence organisation. It was close to impossible to extradite a man under complete surveillance from inside the USSR boundaries.

The book is wonderfully written and reads like a fast paced thriller. It is a well researched account detailing the workings of some of the most dangerous intelligence organisations in the world. It describes how propaganda, fear and paranoia are seeped into the public and details the creation and moods of an empire thus created.

Title: Homegoing
Author: Yaa Gyasi
My Review:
“What I know now, my son: Evil begets evil. It grows. It transmutes, so that sometimes you cannot see that the evil in the world began as the evil in your own home. I'm sorry you have suffered. I'm sorry for the way your suffering casts a shadow over your life, over the woman you have yet to marry, the children you have yet to have.” #yaagyasi


HomeGoing traces the story of the descendants of two half sisters: Effia and Esi, both born in the 18th century Ghana. One was sold to slavery and the other was married to a slave trader.

The book follows the path of their descendants for 6 generations from that point to the present time. Each chapter alternating between the descendants of the sisters. It is amazing how such a complex work is presented with simplicity.

It traces in rich detail how the slave trade began, what fostered it and the unimaginable conditions in which people were sold to America. It shows how the lives of generation after generation is deeply affected from that simple difference in starting points.

The book touches the evolution of black identity in the United States and the effects borne by the people of Ghana due to slave trade particularly since they were a part of the trade in the beginning.

Yaa Gyasi writes with emotion and elegance. The amount of research that went behind for historical accuracy is noteworthy too. Read Homegoing to know and to understand what was and what is.

PS: “Just because someone sees or hears or feels something other folks can't, doesn't mean they're crazy. My grandma used to say, ‘A blind man don't call us crazy for seeing’..”

Title: Enchantress of Florance
Author: Salman Rushdie
My Review:
“Witchcraft requires no potions, familiar spirits, or magic wands. Language upon a silvered tongue affords enchantment enough.” #salmanrushdie

Another masterpiece by Salman Rushdie blending magical realism to history. It tells the story of a young European who visits Akbar’s court and claims that he is the long lost relative of the Mughal emperor.

The author brings to life 16th century Fatehpur Sikri and Renaissance Florence in vivid landscapes, sounds, smells, symbolism and people. The story itself so rich in detail, is hard to distinguish between facts and Rushdie’s exquisite imagination. The work explores the art of story telling that has an unusual importance in human life. We tell stories to understand us better.

The florentine attempts to bring to life the existence of the long lost Mughal princess. But can he convince Akbar that the princess is indeed his mother ?

Akbar consumed by his questions on religion, fate, power to achieve a world of religious tolerance, open culture and what it means to be a just ruler, is taken by his court as a confused man.
But Akbar, turns out be a wonderful listener and patiently follows the story through to the end (much to the worry of the court who feel that the traveller may manipulate the emperor with his stories) and uses his insights to deduce the correctness of the claim.

It is a little hard to follow because of it’s heavy magical realism and many stories intertwining, albeit I could not help but marvel at this fable steeped in history. The book is a juxtaposition of many topics.
You will either love this book or absolutely hate it. This book offers no middle ground.

PS: Salman Rushdie says that this book is his most researched work till date.

Title: The Last Mughal: The Fall of a Dynasty: Delhi, 1857
Author: William Dalrymple
My Review:
“Humne maana ki dakkan mein hai bahut qadre sukhan; Kaun jaaye Zauq par Dilli ki galiyan chhod kar ” #zauq

(We hear that poetry is greatly valued in Deccan these days but, Zauq, who could bear to leave behind the alleyways of Delhi).
—Mohammad Ibrahim Zauq
19 century poet and tutor to Bahadur Shah Zafar

Dalrymple gives a powerful retelling of the course of events that led to the mutiny of 1857 and the last days of the Mughal capital from material that include previously untranslated Urdu and Persian manuscripts, records of Delhi courts, police and administration during the siege, known as the Mutiny papers. The book is the first to present the Indian perspective to the siege and not just from the British sources which to date it has usually been viewed.

The pluralistic, highly refined and philosophically composite culture in Delhi was rooted out permanently after the events of 1857.

It was the memories of 1857 that assisted in the birth of Indian nationalism. Despite numbers and ammunition on our side, Delhi was lost to British simply because of a lack of strategy and coordination among the many factions that made up the mutineers.

But 90 years later, it was not any Mughal descended or any princely or feudal rulers that would lead us to our independence.
Instead the renewed walk to freedom was led by a class of people who were by and large English language and western educated and would use structures, techniques and strategies that are an amalgam of Indian and western philosophy to gain our freedom.


“Umar bhar Ghalib ye hi bhool karta raha,
Dhool chehre par thi aur aaina saaf karta raha! “ #ghalib

(ln your life, O Ghalib, you repeated the same mistake:
your face was dirty but you kept obsessively cleaning the mirror!)
—Mirza Ghalib, 19th century court poet of Bahadur Shah Zafar

Title: Home Fire
Author: Kamila Shamsie
My Review:
“For girls, becoming women was inevitability; for boys, becoming men was ambition “ #khamilashamsie

Home fire introduces us to the life of Muslim immigrant families settled in UK. We meet Isma who raises her twin siblings: Aneeka and Parvaiz after the death of their mother and grandmother. Living under the dark legacy of a dead father who had joined ISIS, and thereby declared a terrorist, Isma struggles to live and raise her family in the aftermath of her father’s choices .

Home fire, is a dark story about how strength, a clear head and resistance to manipulation during your vulnerability is a rare trait, one which you do not inherit, one which you cannot teach, you can only hope that your life choices itself would be a message that your loved ones would imbibe.

Just like in Donna Tartt’s ‘The Secret History’, Khamila Shamsi gives a disturbing visualisation of how closed room ‘secret’ conversations manipulate vulnerable people. And ultimately how this manipulation distorts reality and shakes your priorities. When the bubble breaks, your choices would have already made irreversible changes.

Khamila Shamsi, writes sharply and gently about identities as an immigrant, terrorism, radicalisation, manipulation and the love, grief, strength that goes in maintaining your family.

Even though towards the end, I felt it became a little too dramatic, the parts of Isma and Parvaiz were especially spectacular.

Title: A General Theory of Oblivion
Author: José Eduardo Agualusa
My Review:
“I realise I have transformed the entire apartment into a huge book. After burning the library, after I have died, all that remains will be my voice. In this house all the walls have my mouth” #joseeduardoagualusa

Based on true events, Agalusa tells the story of a Portuguese woman who bricks herself inside her apartment on the night of Angolan independence from the Portuguese. She lives the next 30 years luring pigeons to eat, burning furnitures and books to keep alive, growing vegetables in her terrace and writing her story on the walls with charcoal.

We are shown post-independence Angola unfolding through the eyes of this woman as she catches snippets of conversations from her oblivious neighbours , random news from her radio and from watching people discreetly through her window.

Originally written in Portuguese, it’s translation to English by #danielhahn reads beautifully with a poetic quality to the diary entries of protagonist.

The story meditates on the ways and time it took for the agoraphobic protagonist to slowly, very slowly unbox her fears and step out, iterating that sometimes only forgetting helps you forgive and take the next step.

Title: The Color of Magic (Discworld, #1; Rincewind, #1)
Author: Terry Pratchett
My Review:
‘But what do you want to sacrifice us for?’ asked Twoflower.  ‘You hardly know us!’
‘That’s rather the point isn’t it?  It’s not very good manners to sacrifice a friend.’

Pratchett’s fantastic alternate geography where the world is a flat disc carried on the backs of four big elephants on a giant turtle swimming through space.

We have a Big Bang theory, steady state theory and ‘astronauts’ planning their first manned mission to determine the sex of the turtle 🐢.

Although not Pratchett’s finest work, it introduces us to his style of writing, satire and wonderful imagination.

A nice hot chocolate and Terry Pratchett is a perfect way to spend a Saturday.

Terry Pratchet is to fantasy, what Adam Douglas is to science fiction

PS: The colour of magic is Octarine

Title: Legends of Khasak
Author: O.V. VIJAYAN
My Review:
“The gods are often more unwise than men” #OV Vijayan

The legends of Khasak, a much acclaimed debut work by writer OV Vijayan in 1969 is originally a Malayalam language literature titled ‘Khasakinta Itihasam’ translated to English by the author himself.

Protagonist Ravi, comes as a primary school teacher in a beautiful fictional hamlet in Palghat, Kerala named Khasak.

Khasak is a multi religious community with essence of communism just beginning to permeate in the 1960’s. The writer introduces Khasak through vignettes of beautiful characters. Appu-kili the dragon-fly catcher, Mymoona the village beauty, the fabled goddess of the tamarind tree, Allapichcha the madrassa teacher, Khazi the mystic and Kuttadan the village priest/oracle colour the eccentric and beautiful hamlet of Khasak.

People of Khasak live together with their own shared traditions, history, beliefs and magic irrespective of their personal religion. Not because they are inherently peace loving but simply because it doesn’t make sense not to.
Ravi and the school are the only modern aspects of this beautiful hamlet. But the community is open to Ravi as they have been to others. The legends, fables and green of Khasak was open to any one and for however long you wanted.

Kerala has always been beautiful and OV Vijayan’s dense imagery only makes me homesick. The monsoon, summer, swaying palm fronts and dense greens of this place spread outside the confines of book and accumulates in the lining of your skin.

The original Malayalam book treats you to the dialects of the characters, a mix of Tamil and Malayalam spoken by the Muslims and Hindus of Palghat which is lost in translation. OV Vijayan points out that the English version is more of a stand alone work rather than direct translation and should be treated as such.

Title: The Little Friend
Author: Donna Tartt
My Review:
“It’s awful being a child,” she said, simply, “at the mercy of other people” #donnatartt

One Mother’s Day, 9 year old Robin is found hanging from a tree. The little friend is a story from the perspective of 12 year old Harriet, Robin’s younger sister, who struggles to grapple with the weight that cripples her family since that fateful day 12 years ago.

It is not a fast paced murder mystery novel (even though the synopsis behind the book feels so). It’s a slow read and you cannot race through the pages. An impatient mindset would not work with this book.

The death of Robin is simply the background that sets the undertone for the character of Harriet. The story points to the consequences that arise when children find themselves emotionally abandoned in the world of adults.

Even though its not an easy read and it’s pages of background and character description with little to no dialogues can test your patience, I found it a compelling read.

Title: Whereabouts
Author: Jhumpa Lahiri
My Review:
‘ … I’m amazed at our impulse to express ourselves, explain ourselves, tell stories to one another. ‘ #jhumpalahiri

There is an unnamed woman. There is an unnamed city. ‘Whereabouts’ walks you through this woman’s vignettes: her contemplations, her solitude, her little satisfactions, her familiar spaces, her vague joys and sorrows and her little projections on other nameless characters.

It’s a simple, beautiful writing with no nouns. Each small chapter feels like a letter sent to you as she visits places in her neighbourhood, meets other nameless characters , a letter about intimately insignificant episodes from her life.

At the end of the book. It feels like you read a collection of postcards from a person you have known, over the years. You don’t need their name or address or details. You have known them all your life.

Just as ‘Unaccustomed Earth’, it is not sad or depressing but a beautiful melancholy pervades Lahiri’s words.

PS: ‘Solitude demands a precise assessment of time, I’ve always understood this. It’s like the money in your wallet: you have to know how much time you need to kill, how much to spend before dinner, what’s left over before going to bed.’ #jhumpalahiri

Title: Normal People
Author: Sally Rooney
My Review:
“No one can be independent of other people completely, so why not give up the attempt, she thought, go running in the other direction, depend on people for everything, allow them to depend on you, why not.” #sallyrooney

Set in Ireland, ‘normal people’ is a story of Marianne and Connel and their on-again, off-again relationship which is on and off due to complicated miscommunications.

I understand that the book is popular but I found it very hollow. Marianne and Connels relationship felt too dramatic for my taste. The characters have an arc but no layers.

Marianne and Connel’s relationship to other friends is something I found enjoyable. The subtleties of life in school and college: the boundary between jokes and bullying, demands of friendship and cravings for social acceptance is well captured in the book.

The story might be assimilated better if you look at it as if you are witnessing two people’s choice of relationships. You probably don’t know them or don’t care, but you are a witness and hence watch without thinking.

The authors style is simple and effortlessly fluid which makes it an easy read.
I think you either love this book or you don’t. Unfortunately it did not resonate with me.

Title: Unaccustomed Earth
Author: Jhumpa Lahiri
My Review:
…she made tea. It was a ritual she liked, a formal recognition of the day turning into evening inspite of the sun not setting.” #jhumpalahiri

The book is a collection of short stories which lays bare the inner lives of Indian immigrants in USA. It deals with the theme of cultural separation and identity, the first generation of immigrants face while the second generation grow and assimilate to the new country, indifferent to their parent’s struggle to fit in. The characters forge a new life in the wake of their diminishing memories that clash with the new customs and the growing need to feel home.

Things we have heard but never knew what it felt like, has been given a form. Once you see, you cannot unsee it. You read and understand as if you knew all along.

There is a pervasive melancholy that hangs around the words and yet it’s not a sad book. If your abstract thoughts are an ocean, then Lahiri scooped them right out into a bottle and gave it a form, a shape and a colour.

PS: My favourite from the collection is ‘Unaccustomed Earth’ and ‘Hell-Heaven’.

Title: I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (Maya Angelou's Autobiography, #1)
Author: Maya Angelou
My Review:
“ She said that I must always be intolerant of ignorance but understanding of illiteracy. That some people, unable to go to school, were more educated and even more intelligent than college professors. She encouraged me to listen carefully to what country people called mother wit. That in those homely sayings was couched the collective wisdom of generations” #mayaangelou

I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings is a memoir by Maya Angelou where she captures the loneliness of her childhood, the brutality of racial segregation and of all the things that happened to her from the point of view of a young Maya.

But there is much to smile over too, often in the form of her wry humour, her precocious brother, her strong and deeply religious grandmother (Momma), her beautiful ‘Mother dear’ and from all the books she read as a child.

The book has so many defining moments that slowly shapes Maya and the reader. It is hard to separate yourself from the book and you painfully and joyously live through the childhood with Maya.

The book is authentic and essential and will stay with you.

Title: Strange Weather in Tokyo
Author: Hiromi Kawakami
My Review:
Also titled as ‘The Briefcase’, it’s a story of a relationship between a lonely middle aged woman and her equally lonely high school teacher starting from their chance meeting at a bar.

The book attempts to emotionally elaborate everyday social interactions but doesn’t quite reach the expectation and settles for a mediocre character development.
The unconvincing characters are compensated by description of food and season to mark the changing flavours of their relationship and sets the tone for a warm, matured, simple and cozy loneliness which the characters try to fill.

The not so layered characters made it hard for me to enjoy the story arc but feel free to give it a try if the synopsis intrigues you!

Title: Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
There is no silence without a cry of grief, no forgiveness without bloodshed, no acceptance without a passage through acute loss. That is what lies at the root of true harmony.’ #harukimurakami

Tsukuru Tazaki had 4 friends in high school whose last names had colors in them. Tazaki was the only last name with no color.

One fine day, his friends cut him off the group. The story is Tazaki’s life from that moment to his adulthood. He falls into deep depression and reality is blurred.

I can sense Murakami’s style here. The reader is presented with many instances and characters, most of which slowly fade as you progress.
Do they contribute to the main plot? Probably not, or probably yes. Was he simply hallucinating? Which aspects are real?

I feel that Murakami’s books have unreliable protagonists whose identities and psychology develop as you move along the plot line. What you believe happened is basically how much you rely on the protagonist’s point of view.

That can make this book hard to put down, at the same time very frustrating to read because you sometimes fail to see the relevance of certain parallel story lines.

The plot may not resonate with you, even the characters may not be to your liking, but despite all of this, you somehow experience the character’s solitude and loneliness.

PS: ‘Every person has their own color ‘

Title: South of the Border, West of the Sun
Author: Haruki Murakami
My Review:
“What we needed were not words and promises but the steady accumulation of small realities.” #harukimurakami

Simple, minimalist story of a man who uses his past to justify his choices in the present.
Sabotaging the now by quoting your past and the if’s and probably’s of your life, only hurts the people who share your present.

This is my first murakami book and it feels like a good start. Lyrical quality to writing and complex character development make it a good read.

The protagonist is not my favourite character but I think the book is a good study of how the fragility of human beings lead them to spend an entire lifetime mulling over their choices and how that very act becomes the catalyst that accelerates the destruction of themselves and those around them.
It takes effort and pure strength to understand that you are the accumulation of your choices and that we need to constantly adapt to live with ourselves.

Title: A Strangeness in My Mind
Author: Orhan Pamuk
My Review:
“Now he knew what it was that he wanted to tell Istanbul and write on its walls. It was both his public and private view.
It was what his heart intended as much as what his words always meant to say.

He said it to himself: ‘I have loved Rayiha more than anything in this world’ “

It is a simple story that explores the city of Istanbul from the point of view of Mevlut, his friends and family, just as much as it explores the lives of the characters.

Mevlut struggles to place his actions and thoughts together. All his life, he wonders if he has done what his heart says or simply like the teeming millions around him, spoke of one and did something else. He consciously tries at every point to align his thoughts and actions.

The book has beautifully captured the complex emotions of the mundane struggles of life.

Title: Poor Economics: A Radical Rethinking of the Way to Fight Global Poverty
Author: Abhijit V. Banerjee
My Review:
Why would a man who doesn’t have enough to eat buy a television?
Why is it so hard for children in poor areas to learn even when they attend school?
Why do the poorest people have more children even when they cannot afford it?
Does having lots of children actually make you poorer?
Where are the insurance companies for the poor?

Poor Economics iterates that the lives and choices of the poor tell us about how to fight global poverty.
Through rigorous research and randomised control trials they speak about where existing policies fail, how the poor manage their expenses, how they prioritise and based on these understanding, how to increase the impact and improve the lives of the poor.

Good politics may or may not be necessary for good policies; it is certainly not sufficient, says the duo.
So as we are constantly asked to believe, politics doesn’t always trump policies. Good policies can be a first step to good politics

Title: Azadi: Freedom. Fascism. Fiction.
Author: Arundhati Roy
My Review:
James Baldwin once said, “I love America more than any other country in this world, and, exactly for this reason, I insist on the right to criticize her perpetually.”

Arundhati Roy does exactly the same. She is fierce, unafraid and polarising as any person who fearlessly critiques and documents the powerful.
Roy’s India is not pretty. She bares India’s crumbling infrastructure, colonisation of institutions and a dangerously vast network of misinformation that slowly poisons India’s present and past.

Azadi is a collection of essays and speeches covering the contemporary political turbulence in India and demonstrates how India is witnessing the rise of fascism in her soil.

She dares to bear witness, question, talk and document the ground realities of the country in her unique language and calls for freedom with responsibility and writes what probably no one else will and if no one did, then history of contemporary India will be devoid of perhaps many important events.

Title: The Boy in the Striped Pajamas
Author: John Boyne
My Review:
“What exactly was the difference? He wondered to himself. And who decided which people wore the striped pajamas and which people wore the uniforms?”

Set during the Holocaust of Second World War, ‘The boy in the striped pyjamas’ unfolds a sweet friendship between Bruno and Shmuel, separated by a fence. For a short period, the pair’s innocence hides the brutality that segregates them, offering a unique perspective of a 9 year old to the most hideous conscience of mankind.

Title: Beloved
Author: Toni Morrison
My Review: A devastatingly tragic history written both in subtle poetry and dense metaphors, Toni Morrison’s language will stay with you even after the book.

Title: The Bluest Eye
Author: Toni Morrison
My Review:
“And fantasy it was, for we were not strong, only aggressive; we were not free, merely licensed; we were not compassionate, we were polite; not good, but well behaved. We courted death in order to call ourselves brave, and hid like thieves from life. We substituted good grammar for intellect; we switched habits to simulate maturity; we rearranged lies and called it truth”

Morrison’s debut work poetically talks about self-worth; poverty; finding drops of joy in a wave of sorrow and perceptions of beauty told through a fragile eleven year old Pecola.

Pecola prayed everyday without fail for blue eyes because she ardently believes that would make her beautiful. She doesn’t desire a fairer skin or lighter hair, instead she believes her eyes which captures all her pain and sees the way people look at her, only if they were more beautiful, perhaps the world would react more kindly to her.

What happens to Pecola can only be understood as a past that ruthlessly interconnects and accumulates across generations to form the present. To have written such a thing as your first novel is unbelievable.

Title: Nocturnes: Five Stories of Music and Nightfall
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
Ishiguro’s pet theme of inevitable stillness of life and sense of missed opportunities is reflected in this collection as well.

The author subtly explores a deeper understanding of what it means to be a genius, it’s limitations and about relationships that exist for convenience rather than love.

At the end a disturbing question permeates the stories “Is it worth every sacrifice to try and reach for a passion in life?”

Title: When We Were Orphans
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
Christopher Banks, is 1930 England’s best known detective. Brought up in Shanghai, he was forced to return to England after the disappearance of his parents one after the other when he was 10.

Typical of Ishiguro’s style, Christopher is an unreliable narrative. As you read you notice the difference in how he sees and remembers his life and how his friends and colleagues recall him.

While on the surface it reads like a detective story where the protagonist is trying to find his parents, the book is more than that. We are inside the head of Christopher banks. What we read is not what actually is. We see him living and believing that the incident did not affect him. We watch as he convinces himself (and us) that his choices have to do with more grander reasons than the unresolved case of his missing parents.

At the end, much much later, perhaps when you feel it’s too late, Christopher accepts what is and moves on. This is where Ishiguro shines. When the protagonist finally accepts, it doesn’t mean happiness. But a sort of melancholy contentment and peace.

Just as his previous works, #theremainsoftheday, #neverletmego, his writings begin with a sense of calm restraint and ends with an unsettling sadness, driving home the message that regrets and loss are inevitable in life and perhaps what is required of us is to accept the humanness of it and live on.

Title: The Remains of the Day
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
“What is pertinent is the calmness of beauty, its sense of restraint. It is as though the land knows of its own beauty, its own greatness, and feels no need to shout it.” #Kazuo Ishiguro

It is this sense of restraint that characterises ‘Remains of the Day’. A seemingly calm story-telling that culminates in an unsettling sense of sadness.
Pages and pages subtly peal layers of mastered discipline and dignity of life, unveiling a pervasive sense of melancholy.

Title: Never Let Me Go
Author: Kazuo Ishiguro
My Review:
“It was like when you make a move in chess and just as you take your finger off the piece, you see the mistake you've made, and there's this panic because you don't know yet the scale of disaster you've left yourself open to”- Kazuo Ishiguro

A subtle tale of identity, friendship and power of memories.
It's inevitable that in life people will fail one another, grow old with regrets and fall to pieces. In such an erosion of hope, it asks readers to consider what it really means to be human.

Title: The Fellowship of the Ring (The Lord of the Rings, #1)
Author: J.R.R. Tolkien
My Review:
“In a hole in the ground, there lived a hobbit…..”
What a wonderful world Tolkien has weaved in words. Just like Harry Potter, the trilogy preserves my childhood in its words. Like a friendly greeting from back in time: every word is a portal to my 12 year old self’s thoughts.

I was 12 when I first came across ‘Lord of the Rings’ trilogy. Back then, I relied on public libraries, school and some very generous friends to get my hands on books. This also meant that I had limited time to read.

I started with part 2, ‘Two Towers’ (because I could only get my hands on this one and didn’t want to wait longer to start sequentially).
I found it a tough read (partly because I started with book 2 and partly because I was too young to keep pace with Mr. Frodo). It took me over a month to complete it.

Just as much as I enjoyed it, I knew I missed something and that I will have to come back and read again to feel complete.

Now 12 years later, I have started again on my journey with the ring bearer. This time I follow the order. I started with ‘The Hobbit’ and now completed ‘The Fellowship Of The Ring’.

Author: J.R.R. Tolkien
